key_claim: Bird migration was a mystery for centuries, from moon theories to arrow storks to banding, and modern tracking now lets scientists see journeys almost in real time.

slides.headline: Where do birds go? Some said the moon.
Storks arrived with African arrows
slides.body: In the early 1800s, white storks turned up in Germany with African arrows in their bodies. They were strong evidence that birds travel to Africa and back.

slides.headline: Banding left the middle invisible
slides.body: Of more than 79 million banded birds, only about 6.5 million were found again. The journey between stayed invisible.

slides.headline: Now we can watch the journey
slides.body: Today it's possible to see journeys almost in real time. Tracking devices now fit on smaller birds and record their movements, sending them to receivers or satellites.

slides.headline: We once guessed. Now we can follow.
slides.body: Knowing where birds go helps show where conservation can make a difference.

caption:
Where do birds go? Some said the moon.

For more than 2,000 years, people asked where birds go. Some thought they changed into other species, hibernated underwater or flew to the moon. Then white storks arrived in Germany with African arrows in their bodies.

The catch? Bird banding only showed where a bird was marked and where it was found again. Of more than 79 million birds banded, about 6.5 million have been recovered. Everything between stayed invisible.

The payoff? Tracking devices now fit on smaller birds, and scientists can see journeys almost in real time. That knowledge helps show where conservation can make a difference. 🐦

Source: The Conversation — For centuries, bird migration was a mystery – a tech revolution is changing that, and could help save these amazing creatures
